title: Boats & Canal
strapline: Load the barge, work the lock, and chug along a waterway that goes wherever the children steer it.
intent: Children explore floating and sinking with a real reason — the cargo has to stay dry and the boat mustn't tip.
Children work a simple lock and see cause and effect: water in, boat up; water out, boat down.
Children narrate a slow journey along the canal, naming what they pass — the bridge, the tunnel, the mooring.
Children count and balance cargo, testing how much a boat can carry before it goes under.
Children connect to real waterways and the people who live and work on them.
implementation: Run a water channel — guttering, a builder's tray or a real tuff-spot river — and provide boats that genuinely float.
Offer cargo to load — corks, pebbles, little animals — and let children discover the tipping point for themselves.
Build a simple lock from two blocks and a jug, and pour to raise and lower the boat, narrating what the water does.
Name the journey as they steer: 'under the low bridge, mind your head, into the dark tunnel, out the other side'.
Set floating experiments alongside: which materials float, what happens when we add a passenger, why did that one sink?
Add barge-people, washing lines and a tiny cabin so the canal has a life and a story.
Share pictures or a walk to a real canal, river or harbour and talk about what the boats were carrying.
key_questions: How much cargo can your boat carry before it sinks?
The water came up — what happened to the boat?
Why do you think that one floated and this one went straight down?
What will your barge pass on its journey down the canal?
How could you get your boat under that low bridge?

impact.text: Children explore floating, sinking and balance, loading cargo and finding the point where the boat tips.
Children work the lock and talk about cause and effect — water in makes the boat rise.
Children count and share out cargo and compare which boat carries more.
Children narrate the journey with positional language — under the bridge, through the tunnel, alongside the bank.
Children ask why boats float and sink and predict what will happen next.
Children talk about real canals, rivers and the people who work the boats.
Children pour, scoop and steer with growing control of hands and tools.

enhancements: Guttering and a water channel that runs downhill into a bucket.
A homemade lock — two bricks and a jug — for raising and lowering boats.
A tray of materials to test: cork, foil, sponge, stone, wood — which float?
Little barge-people, animals and washing lines to give the boats a story.
A low cardboard bridge and a dark tunnel the boats must pass through.
Pictures of a real canal, narrowboat or harbour, and cargo to name.
Pipettes and jugs for topping up the water and making currents.

playing_exploring: Children experiment freely — more cargo, a bigger boat, a faster current — to see what happens.
They explore water with their whole selves, splashing and pouring and steering.
active_learning: Children keep reloading and re-launching until the boat carries the cargo without sinking.
Working the lock takes patience — pour, wait, watch the boat rise.
creating_thinking: Children predict which materials float and test their ideas.
They invent journeys and solve the low-bridge, deep-water problems along the way.
